text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Unemployment in Copenhagen is currently falling at the fastest rate in the past 20 years but many jobless still experience major difficulty getting work, leading the city council to set up better training programmes for immigrant workers in particular.
--The Social Democrat-led government calls for greater bureaucratic control and a bigger say for the Finance Ministry in other ministries' activities in a new public sector policy document.

--Danish Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft wants tighter control over local authority spending and the 50 billion crowns the state and municipal authorities invest every year with cleaner water, air, better public transport, schooling, training and research taking priority over investment in culture, motorways, social housing and energy over the next 15 years.

--The ruling Social Democrats are now hinting they might hold a national referendum in Denmark on the result of IGC (the intergovernmental conference on the future of the European Union) in 1998 at the latest. The High Court may not have ruled by then on a constitutional case brought by 10 Danes against the state to prove that Denmark's adhesion to EU treaties is in violation of the country's constitution. The case has been held up due to technical and legal hiccups and the Social Democrats are accusing the plaintiffs of deliberately trying to stall proceeedings.

--Danish shipyards risk closure with the loss of thousands of jobs if the European Commission agrees major new subsidies for German and southern European yards, the Danish Shipowners' Association says. The Danish government and the association have launched an offensive against EU aid plans for shipyards in Germany, Spain and Greece.

--U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers says in a new report that telecommunications group Tele Danmark will have to invest abroad if it is to up earnings in the coming years, due to expected marketshare losses in Denmark. Salomon upheld its 'Hold' recommendation for Tele Danmark shares.
